subject: Business Models
title: Wage Theft in Franchises
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Wage Theft in Franchises.

hook.text: McDonald's franchisees have been sued for wage theft more than any other restaurant brand in America.

buildup.text: Under pressure to maintain margins, some franchisees cut corners: unpaid overtime, altered timecards, skipped breaks.

discovery.text: The franchisor sets royalties and mandates costs. Franchisees with thin margins squeeze labor to survive.

twist.text: The 'joint employer' debate: should McDonald's corporate be liable for its franchisees' labor violations?

climax.text: Franchise structures can create conditions where labor exploitation becomes economically rational.

punchline.text: Thin margins, squeezed workers. The franchise model has a labor problem.

quiz.question: Why are franchisees sometimes motivated to commit wage theft?
options: Thin margins from high royalties and mandated costs

details.summary: Wage theft in franchise systems includes unpaid overtime, off-the-clock work, minimum wage violations, and tip skimming. The franchise structure complicates accountability because franchisees operate independently while franchisors set the cost structures that pressure labor budgets.
details.whyItMatters: Franchise wage theft affects millions of low-wage workers. Joint employer lawsuits attempt to hold franchisors accountable for working conditions they influence through cost targets and operational mandates.
takeaways: Franchise wage violations include unpaid overtime, off-clock work, and tip theft
Franchise cost structures from franchisors pressure franchisees' labor budgets
Joint employer lawsuits challenge whether franchisors share liability for labor violations

faq.question: What types of wage theft are most common in franchise systems?
faq.answer: Requiring employees to work off the clock before or after shifts, not paying overtime after 40 hours, altering time records to reduce reported hours, making deductions from paychecks for uniforms or register shortages, and misclassifying employees as independent contractors or managers.

faq.question: Are franchisors legally responsible for franchisee wage violations?
faq.answer: The legal landscape is evolving. Joint employer rulings in some jurisdictions hold franchisors partially responsible when they control scheduling systems, set labor cost targets, or mandate operational procedures that effectively determine working conditions. This area of law remains unsettled.
